title: Given a string s and a pattern p, determine whether s contains any permutation of p as a contiguous substring. Solve it with the fixed-size sliding window pattern and demonstrate with a complete banking mini-project.
shortTitle: Challenge 1: Permutation in a String (Does s Contain a Permutation of p)
keyPoints: Slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern across the source string.
Build a count signature of the pattern using an int[26] or HashMap.
Maintain a matched counter tracking how many distinct characters have exactly the required count.
On entry, increment the character's window count and update the matched counter on crossing.
On exit, decrement the leaving character's count and apply the mirror update to matched.
The window contains a permutation when matched equals the number of distinct required characters.
Time is O(|s| + |p|) with O(1) work per slide; space is O(alphabet size).

s1_definition.oneliner: Slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern and check whether its character counts ever exactly match the pattern's counts.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Permutation in a string** – determines whether any contiguous substring of `s` of length `|p|` is an anagram of `p`.
- **Fixed-size window** – the window width is exactly the pattern length; one character enters on the right and one leaves on the left per step.
- **Count signature** – both the pattern and the window are represented as character-frequency arrays or maps.
- **Matched counter** – tracks how many distinct characters currently have exactly their required count, making each slide O(1).
- **Complexity** – O(|s| + |p|) time, O(alphabet size) space.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, a loan file requires a specific set of approval stamps in specific quantities but in any order. Rajesh scans a ledger of stamps and checks whether any consecutive block of exactly that size matches the required set in some order.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
Fixed-size window: s = "EIDBAOOO", p = "AB"

  need: {A:1, B:1}, window width = 2

  Slide the window:

  ┌───────┐
  │ E   I │ D B A O O O    count not matching
  └───────┘

    ┌───────┐
  E │ I   D │ B A O O O    count not matching
    └───────┘

      ┌───────┐
  E I │ D   B │ A O O O    D:1, B:1 -> not matching AB
      └───────┘

        ┌───────┐
  E I D │ B   A │ O O O    B:1, A:1 -> MATCH!
        └───────┘
        return true

  Combined count array visualization:

  Initial: count = [A:1, B:1, others:0]
  matches = 24 (24 chars already at 0)

  Add 'E': count[E]=-1, matches=23
  Add 'I': count[I]=-1, matches=22
  Remove 'E': count[E]=0, matches=23
  Add 'D': count[D]=-1, matches=22
  Remove 'I': count[I]=0, matches=23
  Add 'B': count[B]=0, matches=24
  Remove 'D': count[D]=0, matches=25
  Add 'A': count[A]=0, matches=26 -> MATCH!
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Permutation in a String asks whether any contiguous substring of the source of length equal to the pattern is an anagram of the pattern. You solve it with a fixed-size sliding window of width equal to the pattern length. A count signature represents the pattern's character frequencies, and the window maintains a matching count. Each slide adds one character on the right and removes one on the left, with constant work per step.

The matched counter is what makes the solution efficient. Instead of comparing full count arrays on every slide, you track how many characters currently have exactly the right count. Each entering and leaving character updates this counter with symmetric logic: approaching the required count increments it, moving away decrements it. When all characters match, the window is a permutation. This turns an O(n * alphabet) solution into a clean O(n) one.

The combined count array technique is a compact alternative: initialize a single array with the pattern's frequencies, decrement on entry, increment on exit, and count how many entries are zero. When all entries are zero, every character has exactly the right count. This same template directly extends to the find-all-anagrams problem by collecting every matching position instead of returning on the first.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to check whether any consecutive block of approval stamps in a loan file's ledger matched the required stamp set in any order. The fixed window with a matched counter gave constant work per slide and a single linear pass per ledger, keeping the audit system responsive even for files with thousands of stamps.

Remember one sentence: slide a fixed-width window the size of the pattern and use a matched counter to detect when the character counts align in O(1) per step.
